reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: Reviewed the resource-review context, the full `SubstanceReferenceInformation` StructureDefinition report, the deterministic aggregate only as a comparison point, and the directly scoped HTTP REST behavior finding. I also checked the local R4/R6 package evidence for the resource identity, R4 maturity extensions, R4 local element shape, absence of the same R6 resource, and the candidate `SubstanceDefinition.relationship` amount/type shape. Shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` behavior findings were considered as context only because this review is for `SubstanceReferenceInformation`, not the base artifacts.

r4Maturity.effectMd: The R4 resource is trial-use/FMM 0 with sparse local `Todo.` definitions. That weakens the standards burden for preserving the old base model, though it does not eliminate migration risk for adopters that stored regulatory or substance-reference data.

overall.oneLineConclusion: R6 removes the `SubstanceReferenceInformation` resource identity, so R4 instances require a resource-level migration or retention strategy rather than per-element compatibility fixes.

reasoning.thesisMd: `SubstanceReferenceInformation` is not a mostly stable resource with a few local breaks. The same-name R6 StructureDefinition is absent, and the R6 package's substance resources are `Substance` and `SubstanceDefinition`. An R4 instance with `resourceType: "SubstanceReferenceInformation"` is therefore invalid to base R6 tooling before any individual child element is considered.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: The practical migration shape is a removed/replaced resource. Implementers must decide whether to keep these records in R4 form, map selected data into `SubstanceDefinition`, or preserve old content through extensions or a local compatibility resource. The local R4 sections (`comment`, `gene`, `geneElement`, `classification`, and `target`) are optional and under-specified, but they are not mechanically covered by a same-shape R6 successor. That makes the migration policy-driven, even if expected deployment is low.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because the resource identity itself is gone, preserving individual R4 child paths would not by itself make old instances R6-valid or restore generated model, validator, serializer, REST, or CapabilityStatement surfaces. The only highly compatible base design would be to retain a deprecated legacy resource shell or equivalent alias, which would carry an obsolete FMM 0, sparsely specified model in R6. On the supplied evidence, additional local compatibility preservation has reduced leverage compared with a clear migration/retention program.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: A less-breaking design exists in principle: retain `SubstanceReferenceInformation` as a deprecated transitional resource or publish a formal compatibility alias while steering new work to `SubstanceDefinition`. That would help legacy adopters, but it is not obviously low-cost because it preserves a removed, draft substance model and would require R6 codegen, validation, search/REST documentation, and mapping rules for data whose intended R6 successor is not confirmed. Lower-cost mitigation is an official cross-version mapping and guidance for unmapped `gene`, `geneElement`, `classification`, and `target` content.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: The direct HTTP finding that the base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises this resource's REST endpoint is in scope, but for this resource it is derivative of the StructureDefinition removal rather than an independent migration driver. The shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` operation and search-parameter behavior findings may affect systems that also exchange this data, but they are not specific to `SubstanceReferenceInformation` and should be handled in the base artifact reviews.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: I agree with the deterministic aggregate's major conclusion (`Yes`, `removed-or-replaced-resource`, `migration-program-dominates`). The independent review adds nuance: the endpoint loss and local element mapping concerns still matter for migration guidance and possible transition support, but they do not change the resource-level posture because the top-level resource identity break already dominates.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: Confidence is high that the same R6 resource is absent. The main uncertainty is the intended official successor path: the supplied packages do not include a cross-version ConceptMap, StructureMap, or ballot note proving that `SubstanceDefinition.relationship` is the intended target for R4 `target` content.

findingConsiderations.title: SubstanceReferenceInformation resource is absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the decisive finding. The R4 concrete resource has no same-name R6 StructureDefinition, so serialized instances fail at `resourceType` and generated APIs/endpoints disappear. FMM 0 makes the removal more defensible, but it also means migration is resource-level, not a child-element patch.

findingConsiderations.title: R4 local content model has no lossless R6 successor mapping
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This finding matters for conversion quality because the old `comment`, `gene`, `geneElement`, `classification`, and `target` sections do not have a confirmed same-shape R6 home. Once the resource removal is accepted, however, this becomes a migration-design chore rather than a separate reason to preserve the old base resource.

findingConsiderations.title: Candidate mapping of target amount/interaction data changes type domain and required context
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The `Range` versus `Ratio` amount mismatch and mandatory R6 relationship type are meaningful only if `SubstanceDefinition.relationship` is the intended successor for R4 `target`. That candidate mapping could require expert judgment or lose interaction detail, so official mapping guidance is needed; the evidence is not strong enough to treat it as an independent base-design break.

findingConsiderations.title: The full base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises many R4 resource REST endpoints
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This directly lists `SubstanceReferenceInformation`, but for this resource the endpoint advertisement loss follows from the resource removal. It would become important if standards authors chose a deprecated legacy resource or endpoint alias, but it does not independently change the migration conclusion.

findingConsiderations.title: Resource $meta-add is removed from R6 core
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: Shared `Resource` behavior changes can affect any implementation that also uses generic metadata operations, but they are not specific to the `SubstanceReferenceInformation` resource and were not scored as resource-level drivers here.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Publish or locate an official R4-to-R6 mapping decision for `SubstanceReferenceInformation`, including whether content maps to `SubstanceDefinition`, extensions, or no base R6 successor. The guidance should explicitly cover `gene`, `geneElement`, `classification`, `target`, and `target.amount[x]`.

If implementation evidence shows real stored R4 data, evaluate a transitional compatibility option such as a deprecated legacy resource/profile or clearly documented local extension strategy. Without such evidence, prioritize migration guidance over preserving the FMM 0 resource in base R6.

caveats: No official cross-version ConceptMap, StructureMap, or ballot rationale was available in the supplied inputs.
No local R4 example instances were found in the reviewed evidence, so adoption and populated-field prevalence remain uncertain.
The `SubstanceDefinition.relationship` analysis is candidate-based and should not be treated as a confirmed successor mapping.
Shared `Resource` and `DomainResource` behavior changes were considered only as context, consistent with the review instructions.
